findings.asked: Complete the circuit for a lamp's voltage-current graph, plot the graph, describe what it shows.
findings.wentWrong: Few got all three circuit marks: the voltmeter must go in parallel with the lamp and a variable resistor in the gap to give a range of readings; careless variable-resistor symbols lost the mark. Graphs were good apart from axis labels, poor scales by the least able, and ruler lines between points instead of a curve. Descriptions talked only of current rising with voltage and ignored the resistance.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Drew the voltmeter across the lamp, the variable resistor in series, a smooth curve, and said the resistance increases as the current rises.
findings.rule: The story of the graph is about resistance, not just current.

findings.asked: Circuit symbols, complete a filament-lamp characteristic, explain why it curves.
findings.wentWrong: Lamp, ammeter and voltmeter symbols were fine but a switch or a fixed resistor was drawn for the variable resistor; label, unit and origin marks were earned; only the most able understood the curve - even those who said the resistance rises could not say why, and the best answers linked it to temperature and more collisions.
findings.rule: The filament heats up, its ions vibrate more, electrons collide more often, resistance rises, so the current rises less for each extra volt.

findings.asked: Ohm's law calculation with a current given in milliamps.
findings.wentWrong: The method was fine but weaker candidates did not convert 600 mA to 0.6 A.
findings.rule: mA to A: divide by 1000 before substituting.

findings.asked: Electrical power over ten minutes, then an Ohm's law calculation in milliamps.
findings.wentWrong: The power formula was recalled but minutes were not converted to seconds; Ohm's law was known but the milliamp conversion was again missed by a significant minority.
findings.rule: Seconds and amps: convert first, then substitute.

findings.asked: Add a voltmeter to a circuit, plot the graph, calculate resistance, state how it changed.
findings.wentWrong: The symbol was known but the voltmeter was often placed in series; a few used a non-linear scale; R = V/I scored for those who recalled it; nearly all saw the resistance increasing.
findings.rule: Voltmeter in parallel across the component; a linear scale on each axis.

ruleToRemember: V = I R with I in amps (divide mA by 1000). Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel across the component, variable resistor to change the current. A metal wire at constant temperature obeys Ohm's law (straight line through the origin); a filament lamp's graph curves because the filament gets hotter, electrons collide more often with the vibrating ions, and the resistance rises.
aStarSignal: Explaining the curve with temperature, collisions and resistance in one causal chain, and drawing the practical circuit correctly without a scaffold.
